issues.legal_issue: A statutory transfer of ownership interests in school property accompanying a limited-period takeover of school management is not protected as a mere management takeover and requires constitutionally compliant compensation.
material_facts: The local authority owned movable and immovable property pertaining to its schools.
The statutory scheme provided for transfer to the State of rights and interests in that property when the schools were taken over, without providing compensation.
The takeover of management was stated to be for a limited period, but there was no provision for automatic retransfer of the property when that period ended.
issues.conclusion: The ownership interests in the school property could not be acquired under Article 31A(1)(b); their transfer was compulsory acquisition contrary to Article 31(2) because no compensation was provided. Section 3(2) of the Aided Schools Act and the amendments to section 59 of the Punjab Municipal Act made operative by section 6 were void and unconstitutional.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31A(1)(b) protects a limited-period takeover of management of property in the public interest or to secure its proper management; it does not protect acquisition of the owner's proprietary interests. Acquisition or requisition of property must satisfy Article 31(2), including its compensation requirements. The Court discussed the purpose of Article 31A(1)(b), inserted by the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1955, and distinguished the decisions in Charanjit Lal Chowdhuri v. Union of India and Dwarkadas Shrinivas of Bombay v. Sholapur Spinning & Weaving Co. Ltd.

predicates.challenge_to_school_takeover: A party challenges a government takeover of schools and property belonging to a local authority.
predicates.ownership_interests_transferred: The government action transfers ownership or other proprietary interests in property, rather than taking over only its management.
predicates.no_compensation_provided: The applicable scheme provides no compensation for the transferred property interests.

issues.definition: When a challenge to a school takeover involves transfer of ownership interests without compensation, the property transfer is unconstitutional.

issues.legal_issue: An emergency takeover cannot be justified on the emergency ground when the record does not establish that an emergency existed.
material_facts: The State took over management of the schools under an emergency proviso without first giving the local authority an opportunity to show cause.
The takeover notification did not indicate that an emergency had arisen.
The State had not laid a foundation in the writ proceedings for an emergency and could not support the claimed emergency with material before the Court.
issues.conclusion: The State could not sustain the takeover under the emergency proviso on the record before the Court.
issues.legal_principle: The emergency proviso to section 5 of the Punjab Local Authorities (Aided Schools) Act permitted a takeover without prior notice only where the State was satisfied that such a course was necessary in the interests of students in an emergency. The State had to establish the factual foundation for relying on that exceptional power.

predicates.challenge_to_emergency_school_takeover: A party challenges a takeover of school management carried out without prior notice on an asserted emergency basis.
predicates.no_emergency_recorded: The takeover notification does not indicate that an emergency existed.
predicates.no_emergency_basis_established: The State has neither laid a foundation for the asserted emergency in the proceedings nor supported it with material.

issues.definition: An emergency-based takeover is not justified when the challenged action records no emergency and the State establishes no factual basis for one.

issues.legal_issue: A statute's retrospective commencement does not, without language making it retrospective, give retrospective effect to a notification issued under it.
material_facts: The Aided Schools Act was deemed to have come into force from an earlier date.
The State's notification taking over management was issued later and contained no language indicating that it operated retrospectively.
The State had taken steps concerning management and school property before the notification was issued.
issues.conclusion: The notification took effect only from its date of issue, and actions before that date concerning assumption of management and vesting of the local authority's property were void and illegal.
issues.legal_principle: A notification is not retrospective merely because the statute under which it is issued has retrospective commencement. Retrospective effect requires express words or appropriate language implying it.

predicates.challenge_to_takeover_notification: A party challenges the temporal effect of a notification taking over school management.
predicates.enabling_statute_retroactive: The statute under which the notification was issued is stated to have retrospective effect.
predicates.notification_lacks_retroactive_language: The notification contains no express words or other appropriate language giving it retrospective effect.

issues.definition: A takeover notification issued under a retrospective statute operates only from its issuance when the notification itself contains no language making it retrospective.

issues.legal_issue: A local authority's resolution agreeing to contributions while expressly retaining its ownership interests does not amount to a resolution transferring management and control of its schools.
material_facts: The local authority resolved to pay contributions and permit the State to use school buildings while retaining its proprietary rights in the buildings and other school property.
The local authority later passed resolutions reversing its position on paying contributions.
The State relied on the earlier resolution as a resolution transferring the schools under the statutory scheme.
issues.conclusion: The resolution did not fall within the statutory provision for a resolution transferring management and control of the aided schools.
issues.legal_principle: The resolution must be read according to its terms. An agreement to pay contributions coupled with an express reservation of proprietary rights is not a resolution transferring the schools under section 3 of the Punjab Local Authorities (Aided Schools) Act.

predicates.challenge_to_claimed_transfer_resolution: A party disputes that a local authority adopted a resolution authorizing transfer of its schools to the State.
predicates.resolution_agrees_to_contributions: The local authority's resolution agrees to make contributions to the State.
predicates.resolution_retains_ownership: The resolution expressly retains the local authority's proprietary interests in the school property.

issues.definition: A resolution agreeing to contributions but retaining ownership does not authorize transfer of the schools.

issues.legal_issue: A retrospective amendment affecting contributions does not authorize recovery of contributions for a period before a non-retrospective takeover notification took effect.
material_facts: The takeover notification was issued after the period for which the State demanded contributions.
The notification did not operate retrospectively.
The State demanded contributions for periods preceding the notification.
issues.conclusion: Even assuming the relevant statutory provisions were valid, the State could not demand contributions for the period before the notification took effect.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 6 of the Aided Schools Act, the amendments to sections 52 and 59 of the Punjab Municipal Act operated upon a qualifying resolution or takeover. Because the takeover notification was not retrospective, those amendments could not support a contribution demand for the earlier period.

predicates.challenge_to_contribution_demand: A party challenges a government demand for contributions connected with schools taken over by the government.
predicates.demand_covers_pre_notification_period: The demand includes contributions for a period before the takeover notification took effect.
predicates.takeover_notification_not_retroactive: The notification taking over management does not operate retrospectively.

issues.definition: When a contribution demand covers a period before a non-retrospective takeover notification took effect, the contribution for that earlier period is unrecoverable.

issues.legal_issue: A law requiring a local authority to contribute its funds to the cost of schools taken over by the State cannot compulsorily acquire those funds without complying with constitutional compensation requirements.
material_facts: The amended municipal law required the local authority to pay annual contributions from its funds toward the cost of schools taken over by the State.
The contributions were compulsory rather than a payment for a cost the State had incurred on behalf of the local authority.
The law made no provision for compensation in respect of the funds taken.
issues.conclusion: The provision requiring the contributions was void and illegal because it contravened Article 31(2); the State could not recover contributions under it.
issues.legal_principle: A compulsory taking of part of a municipal fund by the State is an acquisition of property and must comply with Article 31(2). The Court followed Municipal Committee, Amritsar v. State of Punjab, [1969] 3 S.C.R. 447. It did not decide the separate contention that the legislature lacked competence to enact the contribution provision.

predicates.challenge_to_compulsory_public_contribut: A party challenges a law requiring a local authority to contribute funds to the government.
predicates.funds_compulsorily_taken: The law requires funds to be transferred to the government rather than merely reimbursing a cost incurred on the local authority's behalf.
predicates.no_compensation_provided: The law provides no compensation for the compulsory taking of the funds.

issues.definition: A law compelling transfer of a local authority's funds to the government without compensation is unconstitutional.

issues.legal_issue: Provisions authorizing a local authority to transfer management of aided schools and authorizing a limited-period management takeover are not, by themselves, unconstitutional.
material_facts: The Act allowed a local authority to pass a resolution transferring management and control of aided schools.
The Act also allowed the State to take over management in specified circumstances, including in the public interest, for a limited period.
The Court identified the constitutional defect in the separate provisions that transferred proprietary interests and compelled contributions without compensation.
issues.conclusion: Sections 3(1), 4 and 5 of the Aided Schools Act were not, per se, in conflict with the Constitution, particularly in view of Article 31A(1)(b).
issues.legal_principle: Article 31A(1)(b) permits management of property to be taken over for a limited period in the public interest or to secure proper management. That protection does not extend to separate provisions acquiring ownership interests or funds without complying with Article 31(2).

predicates.challenge_to_school_management_authority: A party challenges provisions authorizing transfer or takeover of management of aided schools.
predicates.provision_authorizes_management_only: The challenged provision authorizes management and control to be transferred without itself transferring ownership interests or compelling a contribution of funds.
predicates.takeover_limited_period: The government takeover of management is limited to a specified period.

issues.definition: A provision authorizing only a limited-period transfer of school management is not unconstitutional per se.
